opus-5.5.text:
I think what makes Tasks powerful is that it's the first time the model gets a sense of time and initiative. Until now, ChatGPT has been purely reactive: you come to it, you ask something, it answers, and then it just sits there until you come back. Tasks flips that a little. The model can reach out to you on a schedule, follow up, remind you, check on something for you. That seems small, but it changes the relationship from a tool you query to something closer to a collaborator that's working on your behalf even when you're not in the chat.

And honestly, simple is the point. We could have shipped something much more complex and agentic, but a lot of what we learned is that people need a really legible, low-stakes entry point to understand what it means for the model to act asynchronously. "Remind me every morning to practice Spanish and quiz me," or "give me a summary of AI news every Friday." People immediately get that. Then they start getting creative with it in ways we didn't anticipate, like using it for accountability, for daily journaling prompts, for tracking things over weeks.

From a research and product perspective, it's also a really nice primitive to build on. Once you have scheduling and the model proactively initiating, you can start composing it with search, with browsing, with memory, and eventually with more capable agents that do longer-horizon work. So I see Tasks as a kind of foundation. It's teaching both us and users how to think about models that operate over time, not just in a single turn, and I think that's where a lot of the real value is going to come from.

r001.rationale: It gives reminders as an example of Tasks, but does not say users requested reminders while believing ChatGPT could not provide them.

r002.rationale: It links scheduling and proactive initiation with the model’s capabilities, including search, browsing, and memory.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so on the surface Tasks is almost embarrassingly simple, right? It's scheduling. You tell ChatGPT "remind me every morning to check the news" or "send me a summary of AI papers every Friday," and it just does that. People looked at it and said, this is a cron job with a chat interface.

But I think that misses what's actually happening. For the entire history of these models, the interaction has been synchronous. You ask, it answers, the turn ends. The model only exists when you're looking at it. Tasks is the first time the product breaks that loop. The model can now act on your behalf when you're not there. That's a really different mental model for users, and honestly for the model too.

And the reason I think it matters more than the feature itself is that it's a primitive. Once you have "the model does something in the future without me prompting it," you can start stacking on top of it. It can check on things, it can follow up, it can notice when something changed. It's kind of the minimum viable version of an agent that has a relationship with time. Most of what we call agents today is still: you kick it off, you wait, it finishes. Tasks is the thing that lets the model initiate.

The other piece is that it's very legible to normal people. You don't have to explain tool use or orchestration. Everyone understands "remind me." So you get people forming the habit of delegating to the model, in the lowest-stakes way possible, and that habit is the hard part. The capability underneath will get much better. The behavior change is what you're actually trying to seed.

So I'd say it's powerful precisely because it's simple. It's the smallest possible step from "chatbot" to "something that works for you," and small steps that change the interaction paradigm tend to end up mattering a lot more than big features that don't.

r001.rationale: The response gives examples of people using Tasks, but does not say users asked for reminders while believing ChatGPT could not provide them or treat that as evidence of demand.

r002.rationale: It describes Tasks as scheduling that lets the model act on its own capabilities over time, including sending summaries, checking things, and following up.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s powerful because it changes the interaction from you always having to initiate something to ChatGPT being able to follow up at the right time. You can say, “Help me practice a language every morning,” or “Remind me to revisit this decision next week,” and that intention carries beyond the current conversation.

The interface is simple, but that shift is meaningful. It starts to make ChatGPT feel less like a place you go to ask a question and more like an assistant that can support you over time.

r001.rationale: The response gives reminder examples, but does not say that users ask for reminders despite believing ChatGPT cannot provide them or treat that as evidence of demand.

r002.rationale: It describes scheduled follow-ups and ongoing support, but does not clearly attribute Tasks’ power to combining scheduling with the model’s general capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the power is that it changes who initiates the interaction. Usually, you open ChatGPT, ask a question, and get a response. With Tasks, you can ask it to do something later or on a recurring basis, so you don’t have to remember to come back and prompt it again.

The interface is simple, but that shift is meaningful. You can say, “Help me practice something every morning,” and turn a one-off conversation into an ongoing routine. It’s a small step toward an assistant that can support you over time.

r001.rationale: The response describes reminders and recurring tasks, but does not say users requested reminders because they believed ChatGPT could not provide them.

r002.rationale: It connects doing things later or on a recurring schedule with using ChatGPT to help practice, describing scheduling combined with the model’s capabilities.
